items.locator: 2024 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline for Lower Extremity PAD — Acute Limb Ischemia: acute hypoperfusion presents with findings including pain, pallor, pulselessness and poikilothermia/coolness and is a vascular emergency requiring rapid recognition and emergency evaluation.
items.version: 2024 multisociety PAD guideline remains current; rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: American Society of Hematology — Emergency Department Management of Sickle Cell Disease / current SCD pain guidance: laboratory values do not correlate with pain severity and cannot confirm or rule out vaso-occlusive pain; verification/testing should not delay prompt analgesia while complications are assessed.
items.version: ASH SCD pain guidance and current quality measures for timely analgesia rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: Sections on recognition/evaluation and Treatment/Management: suspected transfusion reaction requires immediate cessation of the transfusion, notification of the blood bank/treating clinician, assessment/support, and maintenance of IV access with 0.9% saline; acute hemolytic reactions can include chills, back/flank pain and hypotension.
items.version: Current StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf entry available in 2026; source and recommendations rechecked 2026-08-15.

options.A: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep IV access open with 0.9% saline, assess and support the client, and notify the blood bank and treating clinician per protocol.
options.B: Slow the transfusion, give an antipyretic, and continue the same unit while monitoring whether the chills and back pain improve.
options.C: Pause the transfusion, give an antihistamine, and restart the same unit when the symptoms begin to resolve.
options.D: Complete the current unit before notifying the blood bank because stopping early can interfere with identifying the cause of the reaction.

items.rationale: Chills, severe back pain, hypotension, and impending-doom symptoms shortly after a transfusion raise concern for a serious acute transfusion reaction. The priority is to stop the blood product immediately, maintain IV access with normal saline, assess and support the client, and notify the blood bank and treating clinician according to the reaction protocol. Continuing or restarting the same unit is unsafe.

items.locator: American Burn Association Clinical Practice Guidelines on Burn Shock Resuscitation — adult burns ≥20% TBSA: initial crystalloid resuscitation recommendation is expressed as mL/kg/%TBSA, using body weight in kilograms and percentage of total body surface area burned, then titrated to clinical endpoints.
items.version: ABA Clinical Practice Guideline published 2024; current burn-shock resuscitation guideline rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: An adult with a thermal burn involving at least 20% of total body surface area requires initial IV fluid resuscitation. Which client measurements are used in standard burn-resuscitation calculations expressed as mL/kg/%TBSA burned?
items.rationale: The American Burn Association guideline for adults with burns involving at least 20% TBSA expresses initial burn-shock crystalloid resuscitation in mL/kg/%TBSA. Therefore body weight in kilograms and percentage of total body surface area burned are the defining calculation variables. Clinical endpoints such as urine output are used to titrate ongoing resuscitation, but they are not the two variables in the mL/kg/%TBSA calculation.

items.locator: Continuing Education/Introduction and Evaluation/DSM criteria: delirium is an acute disturbance of attention/awareness and cognition developing over a short period with a fluctuating course; evaluate for underlying medical, medication, substance, or environmental causes.
items.version: StatPearls Delirium updated 2026-01-10; current NCBI Bookshelf version rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: FDA — Pulse Oximeter Basics: oxygen saturation is generally 95%–100% for most healthy individuals; lower readings require interpretation with symptoms, clinical status, and known device limitations, and unexpectedly low values should be assessed/confirmed.
items.version: Current FDA consumer/clinical safety information on pulse oximeters; rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: NIH/NLM MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia — Temperature measurement: normal temperature varies; an oral temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F) is clearly febrile and should be interpreted in clinical context.
American Heart Association — Understanding Blood Pressure Readings: normal adult blood pressure is systolic <120 mm Hg and diastolic <80 mm Hg; 118/76 mm Hg meets the normal category.
items.version: Current AHA blood-pressure category guidance; rechecked 2026-08-15.

items.locator: American Academy of Pediatrics — Pediatric Readiness in the Emergency Department: 2026 Technical Report and current pediatric medication-safety policy recommend weighing children in kilograms and prominently documenting kilogram weight for weight-based dosing; when meaningful weight change is reported, obtain a current measured kilogram weight before calculation.
items.version: AAP Pediatric Readiness technical report published 2026; current pediatric medication-safety guidance rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.rationale: Weight-based pediatric medication calculations require an accurate weight in kilograms. Because the family reports recent poor intake and noticeable weight loss, the nurse should obtain and document a current measured kilogram weight before calculating the mg/kg/day dose. Using an older pound weight, estimating from age/height, or substituting a fraction of an adult dose introduces avoidable dosing error.

items.locator: Official Glasgow Coma Scale — What is GCS?/Derived indices and FAQ: eye, verbal, and motor components can yield a composite total from 3 to 15 when all components are testable; 15 is the highest possible total.
items.version: Current official Glasgow Coma Scale educational resource; rechecked 2026-08-15.
